title: How sudden aid cuts shook global health services and research
label: 27 October 2026 · Global Health evidence session
summary: Witnesses from Kenya, Zambia, Ethiopia and international organisations described how abrupt US and other donor funding cuts have disrupted HIV, sexual and reproductive health services, staff and data systems, and damaged research and outbreak detection. They warned that political rollbacks on sexual and reproductive rights have worsened access. Governments are trying integration, domestic resource mobilisation and private-sector partnerships, but witnesses urged a mixed funding approach, protection of multilateral programmes, local partnership and investment in diagnostics, data and the health workforce.

glossary.definition: United States Agency for International Development, a major US foreign aid agency.
The US President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief, a major funder of HIV programmes.
Sexual and reproductive health and rights — services and legal rights related to sex, contraception, abortion and reproductive care.
A UK-funded global programme that supports sexual and reproductive health services in multiple countries.
A UK-funded programme that supported laboratory networking and antimicrobial resistance surveillance in low- and middle-income countries.
Antimicrobial resistance — when bacteria and other microbes stop responding to treatments, making infections harder to treat.
School-based education about sexual health, relationships and rights designed to help young people make informed choices.

chapters.title: A sudden funding shock and immediate consequences
chapters.takeaway: Abrupt US and other donor cuts left clinics, community programmes, staff and national data systems scrambling and in some places led to medicine stockouts and service closures.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We are investigating global health today. To start, please introduce yourselves and your organisations.

turns.speaker: Jerop Limo
turns.text: I run AYARHEP in Nairobi, a youth-focused organisation supporting adolescents living with HIV with clinical links and community support.

turns.speaker: Dr Kaoma
turns.text: I'm Natasha Kaoma, CEO of Copper Rose in Zambia. We work on reproductive and mental health plus youth economic opportunity and community health.

turns.speaker: Abadi Assefa
turns.text: I'm Abadi Assefa of FGAE in Ethiopia, a 60-year family planning organisation working across public, private and refugee settings.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Jerop, what changes have you seen recently and how did government respond?

turns.speaker: Jerop Limo
turns.text: A year ago communities woke to sudden messages: US funding cuts. Clinics and community programmes we relied on were disrupted. Kenya moved quickly to 'integration'—folding HIV and specialised services into ordinary primary care—but that cannot happen overnight and many young people were lost from care.

turns.speaker: Dr Kaoma
turns.text: In Zambia we saw scale vanish. We reached 200,000 people before; now many organisations reach far fewer. Essential community services and dedicated sexual health centres were closed, and thousands of staff lost jobs.

turns.speaker: Abadi Assefa
turns.text: Ethiopia lost a large share of overseas funding. FGAE faced a big budget cut, thousands of staff contracts were affected and we had to withdraw from many community clinics—people lost follow-up, commodities and outreach.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: You also mentioned data — what happened to systems and records?

turns.speaker: Dr Kaoma
turns.text: Large amounts of health data were held on donor servers. When that funding stopped, access to some systems and staff who managed data was lost, raising trust issues and hurting planning.

chapters.title: Political backlash and rollbacks on rights
chapters.takeaway: Cuts were followed by political moves narrowing language and services on sexual and reproductive rights, increasing stigma and reducing access for young people and marginalised groups.

turns.speaker: Tracy Gilbert
turns.text: Have you faced ideological resistance and what can the UK do to counter rollbacks on rights?

turns.speaker: Jerop Limo
turns.text: Yes. Kenyan leaders publicly framed gender narrowly, stigmatising queer people and limiting talk of 'rights'. Organisations offering safe abortion or youth services were attacked and some closed.

turns.speaker: Dr Kaoma
turns.text: In Zambia the word 'rights' was dropped from official documents: SRHR became SRH. 'Gender' language was replaced by narrower terms. Anti-rights movements targeted comprehensive sexuality education and local advocacy capacity has shrunk as groups scramble for survival funding.

turns.speaker: Abadi Assefa
turns.text: We have also seen external actors pushing family-value narratives and influencing parliamentarians and religious leaders. Lack of transparency over some MOUs worries us.

turns.speaker: Monica Ferro
turns.text: At the UNFPA we see a global rise in 'demographic anxiety' narratives that narrow SRHR. The UK can use its diplomatic voice to defend rights and fund evidence-based programmes.

chapters.title: What governments and organisations are trying — and what could help
chapters.takeaway: Countries are pursuing integration, domestic funding and private-sector solutions, but witnesses said those require careful planning, investment in data, workforce and community organisations.

turns.speaker: David Mundell
turns.text: Natasha, any positives from the funding change? Can anything constructive come of it?

turns.speaker: Dr Kaoma
turns.text: Some systems and policies already exist and can be reused. Opportunities include private-sector engagement for supplies, digital training platforms to reduce repeated training costs, and stronger national insurance or modest service fees to raise revenue.

turns.speaker: Noah Law
turns.text: How should FCDO help to build private partnerships, local sourcing and digital data safely?

turns.speaker: Dr Kaoma
turns.text: Invest in data first. Fund tested local health businesses, support data protection laws and platforms, and offer blended finance that combines grants with patient private investment.

turns.speaker: Jerop Limo
turns.text: A positive is that governments have woken up to reliance on donors. They must actualise social health insurance, restore trust in services, and continue to fund community groups and peer educators who bridge clinics and patients.

turns.speaker: Abadi Assefa
turns.text: Ethiopia is pushing domestic resource mobilisation, modest new taxes for emergency response, local manufacturing partnerships and cross-subsidy models in civil society to keep services for those who cannot pay.

chapters.title: Research, diagnostics and the case for mixed funding
chapters.takeaway: Cuts damaged labs, surveillance and long-term research partnerships; witnesses urged protecting diagnostics, AMR surveillance and a mix of bilateral and multilateral funding with strong local partnerships and accountability.

turns.speaker: Dr Salje
turns.text: From the research view, sudden cuts stopped trials and diagnostics overnight. In South Africa TB trials lost funding and patients lost care; that risks more transmission and faster drug resistance.

turns.speaker: Dr de Polnay
turns.text: As MSF, we see downstream effects: when prevention and basic services fail, we receive sicker children—malnutrition cases that could have been avoided with routine care, vaccination and simple treatments.

turns.speaker: Dr Uadiale
turns.text: The Fleming Fund withdrawal left lab networks and AMR surveillance weakened. In Malawi a hospital went months without lab results because the systems and supplies stopped. That undermines outbreak detection and quality of care.

turns.speaker: Noah Law
turns.text: Is multilateral spending enough now that bilaterals have reduced?

turns.speaker: Dr Salje
turns.text: Multilaterals are vital, but scientist-to-scientist partnerships, Newton and GCRF-style funding, and direct support for labs and standards are best delivered through mixed funding. Some research and long-term partnerships need bilateral backing.

turns.speaker: Monica Ferro
turns.text: UNFPA has scaled some work via multilateral channels and partnerships with development banks, but we also hit the ground through local partners. The UK can protect core humanitarian and SRHR funding while pushing multilateral accountability.

turns.speaker: Tulip Siddiq
turns.text: On UN reform: are you worried about merging UNFPA and UN Women?

turns.speaker: Monica Ferro
turns.text: We are waiting on member-state decisions. Our concern is that merging the two agencies risks diluting specialised services for women and SRHR; reform should strengthen, not weaken, those services.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Quickly: what one practical priority would you want the UK Government to act on?

turns.speaker: Dr de Polnay
turns.text: Protect humanitarian and nutrition funding and ensure supplies and frontline services are funded — prevention saves lives and money downstream.

turns.speaker: Dr Salje
turns.text: Keep funding diagnostic labs, reference standards and research partnerships so outbreaks and AMR can be detected early.

turns.speaker: Dr Uadiale
turns.text: Champion rapid, affordable AMR surveillance and support workforce retention at country level.

turns.speaker: Dr Kaoma
turns.text: Invest in data systems, digital training and local organisations — they keep services running when donors leave.

turns.speaker: Jerop Limo
turns.text: Support community-level organisations and peer-led care; they are essential for adherence and reaching marginalised people.

turns.speaker: Monica Ferro
turns.text: Use UK diplomatic weight to defend SRHR language and access, and ensure multilateral funding reaches local partners and midwives on the ground.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you all. Your testimony shows the immediate harms of abrupt funding change and clear priorities for UK and global action: protect basic services and data, back local partners, and maintain research and diagnostics capacity.
